extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, patent agents, inventors, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal rules for drafting, construing, and evaluating patent claims—what language and forms are permissible or fatal, how claims are interpreted with reference to the specification and drawings, and special rules for combinations and joinder of inventions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be clear, definite, and not use ambiguous/useless words
rubrics_metrics.description: The Claim should clearly, definitely, and correctly comprehend the alleged subject-matter of the invention and nothing more; no ambiguous or useless word or phrase ought ever to be allowed in a Claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although courts will sometimes sustain a claim inaccurately expressed if the court can see what the invention really is, applicants should draft claims to be self-sufficient and definite. Ambiguity may sometimes be cured by examining the Description, but claims ought not to rely on vague wording. (Cases cited: Stover v. Halsted; Ex parte Demming.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid indefinite expressions such as 'means' or 'mechanism' for essential elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim cannot use such indefinite expressions as 'means,' 'mechanism,' etc., when referring to essential elements of the patentable subject-matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While the words 'means', 'mechanism', 'connections' may be proper when used to denote appliances which are not part of the invention, they must not be used with reference to essential elements. An apparatus should be claimed as a specific device rather than as a vague 'means of doing'. (See Ex parte Demming; Ex parte Bates.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not expressly claim 'equivalents' or use equivocal/repetitive synonymous words
rubrics_metrics.description: The repetition of synonymous words is improper and equivocal words (such as 'equivalent') must not be used; the insertion of 'equivalent' in a Claim implies matter outside its ordinary meaning and may widen the scope while leaving limits undefined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalents are generally regarded as covered even if not mentioned, so stating 'equivalents' adds nothing and can be harmful. Equivalents should not be expressly claimed unless the equivalents are described in the specification or special circumstances (e.g., mutual blocking patents) make it necessary. Examiners may require deletion of 'or equivalents', and applicants can then insert particular claims for alleged equivalents. (Cases: Burden v. Coming; Ex parte Reid; Ex parte Dolph; Ex parte Johnson.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious with technical phrases like 'as described' and 'substantially as described'
rubrics_metrics.description: Phrases such as 'as described', 'substantially as described', or 'substantially as and for the purposes set forth' refer to the Description and are neither necessary nor inherently limiting; their legal effect depends on the clarity of the Description and the intended limitation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These phrases add nothing to the certainty of a properly drawn claim and may be dangerous if used as substitutes for clear language. 'Substantially as described' has no efficacy unless the Description is clear; 'substantially as and for the purposes set forth' is a words-of-limitation and should be used only when that special signification is intended. 'Mechanism substantially as described' can be too vague. (See Mitchell v. Tilghman; Ex parte Skinner; Ex parte Wilkin; Ex parte Ewart.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim must set out the invention, not merely refer to the Description
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim must set out the invention itself rather than merely refer to or restate the Description; a claim that merely refers to the specification without stating the invention is too vague.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim should be sufficient in its own terms to the specific features set out in the Description. However, in construing the Claim the courts will consider the whole specification and drawings; where consistent, the Description may amplify and explain concise claim language. Drawings cannot replace a written Description such that a claim covers matter shown only in drawings. (See Ex parte Demming; Westinghouse v. Gardner & Ransom; Gunn v. Savage.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim a mere function (functional claims are void)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim for the function of the invention—claiming the producing of an effect rather than the means by which it is produced—is void, since it neither covers a patentable invention nor corresponds with the given Description.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will, if possible, construe participial or functional claims as claims for the means by which the function is performed; apparatus must be claimed as specific devices, not as 'means of doing'. Participial forms like 'producing', 'operating', 'determining' are suspect. Functional language may be acceptable where the invention is itself an art or process and the function is the true invention. (See Ex parte Ives; Matthews v. Schoneberger; Royer v. Schultz; Ex parte Cox.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not claim a mere result/effect (unless the result is itself a new product)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim that claims only the result accomplished by the invention (a mere effect) rather than the invention itself is void, unless the result is a new product constituting the real invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where a result is simply an effect of described means, it is not patentable as a monopolizable subject. Courts often construe such claims, if possible, as claims for the art or instruments producing the effect. Claims for results as products (e.g., a new composition) may be valid. (See Ex parte Beavis; Marsh v. Dodge & Stevenson; Bailey Washing & Wringing Mach. Co. v. Lincoln.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid alternative (disjunctive) claiming that creates uncertainty
rubrics_metrics.description: A Claim stated in the alternative is invalid when its language either covers nothing positively or leaves uncertain which of several things the inventor intends to claim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use of disjunctive conjunctions does not automatically render a claim uncertain if the essential characteristics are properly set forth. Alternatives that merely describe modes or connections may be acceptable; but alternative claims are disfavored by the Patent Office and it is preferable to state separate claims for separate alternatives when practicable. Courts may sustain alternative claims where intelligible. (See Union Paper Bag Mach. Co. v. Nixon; Ex parte Holt.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not unnecessarily multiply claims (avoid redundant or fictitious claims)
rubrics_metrics.description: Repetition of the same Claim or multiplication of claims for the same invention is not allowed except where necessary to describe the invention in different methods to make it clear or to state all that can rightfully be claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unnecessary multiplication tends to mislead by implying substantive differences where none exist and may, if carried too far, create ambiguity that renders the patent void. Where one claim will suffice, no others should be made. Some repetition in different language to prevent misunderstanding may be tolerated, but divided or multiplied claims that appear fictitious or redundant are disapproved. (See Dederick v. Cassell; Carlton v. Bokee.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper joinder of claims for different inventions
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims for different inventions may be joined in the same specification only insofar as the nature and dependence of those inventions permit their joinder; each claim must possess all characteristics and fulfil all requirements necessary to its validity as if it were the sole invention claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are the 'life' of the patent and may embrace every invention for whose protection the applicant may lawfully apply; but a claim for a separate invention must stand on its own merits. A second claim for an inseparable feature of an already claimed invention is improper. (See Ex parte Smith; Combined Patents Can Co. v. Lloyd.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims are interpreted and limited by the specification and drawings (but claims control where conflict exists)
rubrics_metrics.description: In construing a Claim the whole specification is taken together; if the Claim's language is consistent with the Description and drawings, the latter are treated as amplification and explanation, and features declared essential in the Description are covered by the Claim even if not expressly mentioned.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Claim must still be complete in itself and cannot be enlarged by the Description. Drawings may limit a claim where they describe the device by reference letters, but drawings cannot wholly supplant a written Description. When Claims and Description disagree, the Claims control. Courts construe claims in view of the state of the art to render the claimed invention evident to those skilled in the art. (See Snow v. Lake Shore & Mich. S.R. Co.; McKesson v. Camdick; Gunn v. Savage.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination claims must be claimed as combinations and include all essential cooperating elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A combination is an invention distinct from its elements and from the law of their co-operation; a claim for a combination must include all its essential characteristics and embrace enough to produce a distinct and useful result, and must be confined to the union of elements the inventor has created and described.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims for individual elements do not cover the combination; nor does a claim for all elements collectively under a different co-operative law. A claim that includes an element not co-acting as part of the combination is invalid. Combination claims must distinguish clearly between elements and the manner of their co-operation. (See Delaware Coal & Ice Co. v. Packer; Van Camp v. Maryland Pavement Co.)
